claims.text: The varied stress–strain and thermoelastic behaviors of HfNbTaTiZr arise from controlled local compositional heterogeneity.
Local compositional heterogeneity produces differences in local thermal expansion coefficients.
Differences in local thermal expansion produce localized thermal stresses during high-temperature exposure and thermomechanical processing.
Localized thermal stresses modulate creep behavior, elastic moduli, and aging hardening.
The proposed initial homogenized, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
Varying the concentration of Nb, Ta, or Ti while compensating with Hf will create controlled atomically resolved chemical inhomogeneities.
Compositional tuning alters interatomic bonding environments.
Altered bonding environments cause different regions of the alloy to expand non-uniformly when heated.
Thermal-expansion mismatch creates local stress fields that affect dislocation motion and microstructural evolution.
Increasing local heterogeneity, such as by increasing Nb and compensating with Hf, should improve high-temperature creep resistance by hindering dislocation motion.
Increasing local heterogeneity should measurably change the temperature dependence of the elastic moduli relative to a homogeneous baseline.
Increasing local heterogeneity should produce more pronounced aging hardening.
Compositionally heterogeneous samples should show stress–strain curves different from those of the uniformly mixed baseline.
The proposed effects should be most significant above 600 °C for creep and aging phenomena.
Thermal stresses caused by expansion mismatch are critical during cold rolling.
The influence of local thermal-expansion mismatch on HfNbTaTiZr behavior is supported.
